questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on the right hand that started as a papule and progressed to a vesicle, then a black eschar surrounded by non-pitting oedema. Gram stain shows large gram-positive rods in chains. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax presents as the 'malignant pustule' — a painless vesicle that ruptures leaving a black eschar (anthrax means coal/black) with surrounding gelatinous non-pitting oedema. Causative organism is Bacillus anthracis, a large gram-positive rod in chains.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of deeply seated vesicles on palms and soles with intense pruritus. The vesicles are tense, do not coalesce, and recur seasonally. KOH mount is negative. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: This is pompholyx (dyshidrotic eczema). It presents with intensely pruritic, tense, deep-seated vesicles on palms and soles. KOH negative rules out tinea. First-line treatment is potent topical corticosteroids, often under occlusion to enhance penetration.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic presents with a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the foot with crepitus on palpation, foul-smelling discharge, and X-ray showing subcutaneous gas. Which organism combination is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis Type I (polymicrobial) is common in diabetics. It involves synergistic infection with anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridium) and facultative anaerobes/gram-negatives. Gas in soft tissue on X-ray is a classic sign.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with multiple hypopigmented macules on the trunk and upper arms. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (now reclassified as M. globosa/M. restricta). The classic KOH finding is short hyphae and yeast cells resembling 'spaghetti and meatballs'. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child develops grouped vesicles on an erythematous base around the mouth, followed by lesions on palms and soles with painful oral ulcers. The child is febrile. Which virus is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) is caused most commonly by Coxsackievirus A16 (and Enterovirus 71). It presents with fever, oral ulcers, and vesicular lesions on palms and soles in children. Distinguished from herpangina by the peripheral lesions.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with a painless, indurated, clean-based ulcer on the glans penis with rubbery inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark field microscopy shows motile spiral organisms. RPR is reactive. Which stage of syphilis is this?
questions.exp: This is the classic presentation of primary syphilis — a painless, indurated chancre at the site of inoculation with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy. Dark field microscopy shows Treponema pallidum. RPR and TPHA are reactive.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male with urethral discharge and dysuria. Gram stain of discharge shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci within neutrophils. He also has conjunctivitis. What is the treatment of choice for uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea?
questions.exp: Current WHO/CDC guidelines recommend IM ceftriaxone 500mg (or 1g if >150kg) as single dose for uncomplicated gonorrhoea, due to widespread fluoroquinolone resistance. Azithromycin is no longer routinely co-prescribed due to emerging resistance.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT (MB regimen) develops sudden onset fever, painful erythematous nodules on the face and limbs, iritis, and orchitis. Nerve function assessment shows no new deficit. What is this reaction and what is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It is immune complex-mediated and presents with painful erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic involvement. Thalidomide is the most effective treatment (contraindicated in women of childbearing age); prednisolone is used when thalidomide is unavailable.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male has anaesthetic hypopigmented patches on the trunk with palpably thickened great auricular and ulnar nerves. Slit skin smear from lesions is negative. Skin biopsy shows epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytic infiltrate around dermal nerves. What is the leprosy classification?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with few, well-defined, anaesthetic hypopigmented patches, palpably thickened peripheral nerves, negative smear, and histology showing well-formed epithelioid granulomas around nerves with lymphocytic cuffing. Cell-mediated immunity is high.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA is positive (1:640, homogeneous pattern) and anti-dsDNA antibodies are elevated. Urinalysis shows proteinuria. Which HLA type is most strongly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is associated with HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3. HLA-B27 is associated with ankylosing spondylitis, HLA-Cw6 with psoriasis, and HLA-DR4 with rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, puffy fingers, dysphagia, and skin tightening limited to fingers and face (sclerodactyly). ANA shows anticentromere pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc/CREST syndrome) is characterised by Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, and Telangiectasia. Anticentromere antibodies are highly specific for lcSSc. Skin involvement is limited to distal extremities and face.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with flaccid bullae that rupture easily, leaving raw erosions, and Nikolsky's sign is positive. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG and C3 deposition in an intercellular 'fishnet' pattern throughout the epidermis. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is an autoimmune intraepidermal blistering disorder with IgG antibodies against desmoglein 3 (mucosal type) and desmoglein 1 (mucocutaneous type). DIF shows intercellular IgG/C3 in a fishnet/lace pattern. Nikolsky sign is positive.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with tense bullae on an urticarial base involving the trunk and flexures. Nikolsky's sign is negative. DIF shows linear deposition of IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction (DEJ). ELISA confirms antibodies against BP180 and BP230. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune blistering disorder in the elderly. It presents with tense bullae on urticarial plaques. Nikolsky sign is negative (subepidermal). DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at DEJ. Antigens are BP180 and BP230 (hemidesmosomal proteins).

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with intensely pruritic, grouped vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks. Small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy. DIF of perilesional skin shows granular IgA at the DEJ in dermal papillae. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is associated with coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). DIF shows granular IgA in dermal papillae. Dapsone provides rapid symptom relief; long-term management requires strict gluten-free diet which can induce remission.

questions.q: A 65-year-old chronic smoker presents with a 2 cm pearly, telangiectatic nodule with a rolled border on the nose. It occasionally bleeds. The lesion has been present for 2 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. The classic presentation is a pearly/translucent nodule with rolled borders, telangiectases, and central ulceration. Sun-exposed areas of the head and neck are most commonly affected in chronic sun-exposed individuals.

questions.q: A 50-year-old farmer presents with a rapidly growing, well-differentiated squamous tumour on the sun-exposed dorsum of the hand. Dermoscopy shows a keratin mass with looped/coiled vessels at the periphery. What feature histologically differentiates keratoacanthoma from SCC?
opts: Lack of atypia and symmetric crateriform architecture with overhanging lip
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing, self-resolving lesion considered by some as a variant of well-differentiated SCC. Histologically, KA has a crateriform architecture with a central keratin-filled crater, overhanging epithelial lips, and glassy/ground-glass cytoplasm without significant atypia — features that distinguish it from invasive SCC.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman undergoes patch testing. After 48-hour occlusion, one patch site shows erythema, papules, and vesicles. A control site is negative. What type of hypersensitivity reaction underlies this response?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a classic Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitised T lymphocytes (specifically CD4+ Th1 and CD8+ cells). The reaction peaks at 48-72 hours. Patch testing reproduces this reaction to identify the causative allergen.

questions.q: A 30-year-old patient with psoriasis is started on methotrexate. Which baseline investigation is most important before initiating therapy, and which test should be performed at regular intervals?
opts: Liver biopsy; serial liver biopsies after every 1.5g cumulative dose
questions.exp: Methotrexate is hepatotoxic; liver biopsy was previously recommended at baseline and after every 1.5g cumulative dose. Current guidelines prefer serial monitoring with procollagen III peptide (PIIINP) or FibroScan (transient elastography) as non-invasive surrogates. LFTs and CBC are monitored every 1-3 months.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for DLE develops sudden visual blurring and difficulty reading. Fundoscopy shows a 'bull's eye' maculopathy. What is the mechanism of toxicity?
opts: Accumulation in melanin-containing cells of the RPE causing photoreceptor toxicity
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine concentrates in melanin-rich tissues including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Accumulation leads to direct photoreceptor toxicity, manifesting as the classic 'bull's eye' maculopathy. Annual ophthalmology screening (visual field + SD-OCT) is mandatory. Risk increases with >5 years use or >5mg/kg/day.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with a painless, well-defined hyperpigmented plaque on the shin with central clearing and a raised, indurated hyperpigmented border. The lesion feels board-like on palpation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Morphea (localised scleroderma) presents as indurated, hyperpigmented plaques with a lilac ring at the active border. The lesion has 'ivory-coloured' centre, feels woody/board-like, and lacks systemic sclerosis features. It is a localised form of scleroderma without ANA or internal organ involvement.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with purpuric papules on the lower limbs that do not blanch on pressure. Skin biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltrate around small vessels with nuclear dust and fibrinoid necrosis. Urinalysis shows haematuria. What is the pathological diagnosis?
questions.exp: Leucocytoclastic vasculitis (hypersensitivity vasculitis) affects small vessels and presents with palpable purpura. Histology shows neutrophilic infiltrate, leukocytoclasis (nuclear dust), fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls, and red cell extravasation. It can affect kidneys (haematuria/proteinuria).

questions.q: A 35-year-old South Indian male presents with extensive, well-defined hypopigmented macules involving >80% BSA, including lips, nipples, and genitalia. He has premature greying. What investigation best determines the activity of disease?
questions.exp: In vitiligo, dermoscopy showing perifollicular pigmentation (pigment remaining around follicles) indicates residual melanocytes and is a marker of repigmentation potential/disease activity. It also helps in therapeutic decision making. Wood's lamp enhances contrast but does not assess activity.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops a widespread blistering eruption 2 weeks after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. She has >30% BSA epidermal detachment, high fever, and mucosal involvement of eyes, mouth, and genitalia. What is the SCORTEN score used for?
opts: Predicting mortality in toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)
questions.exp: SCORTEN (SCORe of Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis) is a severity-of-illness score that predicts mortality in TEN/SJS-TEN overlap. It scores 7 parameters: age >40, malignancy, tachycardia >120, initial epidermal detachment >10%, serum urea >10mmol/L, serum glucose >14mmol/L, and bicarbonate <20mmol/L.

questions.q: A 50-year-old undergoes a Mohs micrographic surgery for a recurrent BCC on the nose. What is the key advantage of Mohs surgery over standard excision?
opts: Lower cost and shorter operating time
Complete margin assessment with tissue sparing and lowest recurrence rate
Suitable for all skin cancers including melanoma
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery allows intraoperative complete circumferential peripheral and deep margin assessment (CCPDMA) using horizontal frozen sections, mapping the tumour precisely. This results in the highest cure rates and maximum normal tissue conservation — ideal for recurrent, ill-defined, or high-risk BCCs on the face.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs dermoscopy on a pigmented lesion and observes an atypical pigment network, irregular streaks, blue-white veil, and regression structures. According to the 7-point checklist, how many major criteria are present?
opts: 3 major criteria (atypical network + blue-white veil + atypical vascular pattern)
questions.exp: In the 7-point dermoscopy checklist for melanoma, major criteria (score 2 each) are: atypical pigment network, blue-white veil, and atypical vascular pattern. Minor criteria (score 1 each) are: irregular streaks, irregular pigmentation, irregular dots/globules, and regression structures. A score >=3 is suspicious for melanoma.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man with HIV (CD4 60 cells/uL) presents with extensive verrucous, cauliflower-like perianal growths, and smaller flat papules on the shaft. Biopsy shows koilocytes, acanthosis, and parakeratosis. Which HPV types are most associated with the highest malignant potential?
questions.exp: HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk oncogenic types associated with anogenital carcinomas and Bowen's disease of the genitalia. HPV 6 and 11 cause condylomata acuminata (genital warts) and are low risk. HPV 5 and 8 are associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) with risk of SCC.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent painful oral ulcers (3-4 per year), each healing in 10-14 days without scarring. The ulcers are oval, 5mm in diameter, with a yellowish pseudomembrane and erythematous halo. Systemic examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS), minor type, presents with small (< 1cm), oval ulcers with pseudomembranous base and erythematous halo on non-keratinised mucosa. They heal without scarring in 10-14 days. Absence of systemic features distinguishes it from Behcet's disease.

questions.q: A patient on long-term clofazimine for lepromatous leprosy develops orange-red discolouration of skin, tears, and urine. He is concerned. What is the mechanism of this pigmentation?
opts: Deposition of clofazimine crystals in macrophages and skin
questions.exp: Clofazimine is a fat-soluble riminophenazine dye that deposits in macrophages, skin, and other organs. It produces a reddish-brown to orange discolouration that is dose-dependent and reversible on drug withdrawal. Crystal deposition in the skin and mucosa causes the characteristic pigmentation.

questions.q: A 55-year-old presents with a solitary, firm, non-tender, 3cm ulcerated tumour on the scalp with satellite nodules. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is positive. Immunohistochemistry: S100+, HMB-45+, Melan-A+. What is the Breslow thickness significance?
opts: Determines choice of topical vs systemic therapy
Primary determinant of prognosis and surgical excision margins
Used only for non-melanoma skin cancers
questions.exp: Breslow thickness (depth from granular layer to deepest tumour cell) is the most important prognostic factor in primary cutaneous melanoma. It determines surgical excision margins (0.5-2cm based on depth), SLNB indications (>=0.8mm or <0.8mm with ulceration), and T-staging in AJCC 8th edition.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male on HAART for HIV develops multiple violaceous papules and nodules on the lower limbs, palate, and conjunctiva. CD4 count is 150 cells/uL. What is the causative agent and its primary mode of transmission?
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma in HIV is caused by HHV-8 (Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus/KSHV). Transmission occurs via sexual contact (MSM predominantly) and saliva. It presents with violaceous papules and nodules in the epidemic (HIV-associated) form, primarily on the lower extremities, mucosal surfaces, and viscera.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with photosensitivity — a burning sensation within minutes of sun exposure on exposed areas — and urine that turns dark brownish-red on standing. Plasma porphyrins are elevated. Wood's lamp of urine shows coral-pink/red fluorescence. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) results from ferrochelatase deficiency. It causes immediate burning photosensitivity. The dark urine and Wood's lamp coral-pink fluorescence are characteristic of porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) caused by uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency. The question tests recognition of both — EPP for burning photosensitivity pattern and PCT for urine fluorescence.
